summary: Pre-Congestion Notification marks packets when traffic exceeds configured rates. This RFC defines how to encode three PCN states in the IP header using a single Diffserv codepoint, together with ECN bits.

plainLanguage.summary: It fits three different warning levels into the small space in a packet header, using one label and a couple of extra bits.

questions: how are three pcn states encoded in the ip header
pcn encoding with a single dscp
what is threshold marking vs excess traffic marking
subtitle: How three levels of pre-congestion warning ride in the ECN bits of an IP header beside one Diffserv codepoint.

tldr.problem: Pre-Congestion Notification needs up to three marking states on each packet, but the earlier encoding in RFC 5696 gave it only two and left one codepoint experimental.
tldr.mechanism: Within a PCN domain, a PCN-compatible DSCP tells nodes to read the two ECN bits as not-PCN (00), not-marked (10), threshold-marked (01) or excess-traffic-marked (11).
tldr.outcome: RFC 6660 is a Proposed Standard that obsoletes RFC 5696, and it requires tunnel endpoints in the domain to follow RFC 6040.

today: RFC 6660 is a Proposed Standard and obsoletes RFC 5696, whose encoding provided only a subset of the same capabilities. The metadata lists no later RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why PCN Needs an Encoding
sections.content:
Pre-Congestion Notification (PCN) protects the quality of service of inelastic flows, such as real-time traffic, inside a Diffserv domain. The overall rate of PCN traffic is metered on every link, and packets are marked when configured rates are exceeded. Those rates are below the link rate, so boundary nodes hear about overload before real congestion happens.

Two marking functions exist. Threshold-marking marks all PCN packets once their rate on a link exceeds the PCN-threshold-rate. Excess-traffic-marking marks only the packets that exceed the PCN-excess-rate, which is typically larger than the threshold rate. Egress nodes pass the marks on to Decision Points that admit new flows or terminate existing ones.

RFC 5696 encoded two marking states with one DSCP and left the value 01 as an experimental codepoint. Edge behaviours that use both markers need three states, so this RFC turns that codepoint into a third state. It only defines the wire encoding for IPv4 and IPv6 headers and changes no marking or congestion-response algorithm.
sections.plainLanguage: Imagine a road with a gentle 'getting busy' sign and a louder 'jammed' sign. The old scheme had room for only one sign, so this one makes room for both.

sections.title: The 3-in-1 Encoding
sections.content:
A PCN node is configured to recognise certain DSCPs as PCN-compatible. For a packet with such a DSCP, the node reads the two-bit ECN field using the 3-in-1 meanings instead of the RFC 3168 meanings. Packets with other DSCPs, and nodes outside a PCN domain, keep using RFC 3168.

  • 00 (Not-ECT): not-PCN, a packet with a PCN-compatible DSCP that is not subject to PCN metering and marking.
  • 10 (ECT(0)): NM, not marked by any PCN marker yet.
  • 01 (ECT(1)): ThM, marked by a threshold-marker.
  • 11 (CE): ETM, marked by an excess-traffic-marker.

Any packet with a PCN-compatible DSCP and an ECN field other than 00 is a PCN packet. Excess-traffic-marked is treated as more severe than threshold-marked, because the excess rate is configured larger than the threshold rate. A fourth state for 'marked by both' is not needed.
sections.plainLanguage: Two little switches in the header make four settings. One setting means 'ignore me', and the other three mean fine, busy and very busy.

sections.title: Tunnelling Requirements and Where It Applies
sections.content:
The encoding fits networks that use two marking behaviours. It can also be used with only one, in which case one of the codepoints MUST NOT be used anywhere in the domain.

Tunnel endpoints (IP-in-IP and IPsec) in the domain MUST follow the ECN tunnelling rules of RFC 6040. The problem is a legacy decapsulator from before RFC 6040: if a node threshold-marks the outer header of a tunnelled packet whose inner header is not-marked, the legacy endpoint forwards the packet as not-marked and the mark is lost.

There is one limited exception. If any pre-RFC 6040 decapsulator exists in the domain, every PCN node MUST be configured never to set the ThM codepoint, and interior nodes MUST use only excess-traffic-marking. Otherwise the encoding is not applicable.

The codepoint order was chosen as a safety net. Legacy tunnels never propagated 01 but have always propagated 11, so the most severe state, ETM, still gets through an overlooked legacy tunnel.
sections.plainLanguage: Some old tunnels drop the gentle warning but still pass the loud one. So the loud warning uses the code that always gets through.

sections.title: What Ingress Nodes Do
sections.content:
A PCN-ingress-node applies four functions to arriving packets, in this order: PCN-classify, PCN-police, PCN-colour and PCN-rate-meter. Any re-mapping of Diffserv codepoints from another domain MUST happen before this processing.

If a classified PCN packet already has an ECN field other than Not-ECT, it comes from an ECN-capable transport, and the node MUST first apply one of several local-policy actions. Encapsulating the packet in an RFC 6040 IP-in-IP tunnel, or in a lower-layer protocol that can be PCN-marked such as MPLS, is RECOMMENDED, with IP-in-IP as the default. The encapsulation must come before policing and colouring. Passing such packets through unencapsulated while dropping CE-marked ones, or dropping them outright, are both NOT RECOMMENDED.

Packet-level policing blocks packets that could be mistaken for PCN packets: ones that are not classified as PCN, already carry a PCN-compatible DSCP, and have an ECN field other than Not-ECT. The ingress MUST re-mark their DSCP to a non-PCN-compatible one, tunnel them with such a DSCP in the outer header, or drop them (NOT RECOMMENDED). By default it SHOULD re-mark the DSCP to zero. Finally, colouring MUST set a PCN-compatible DSCP and the not-marked codepoint on all PCN packets.
sections.plainLanguage: At the entrance, a guard checks every packet. Real PCN packets get the 'all fine' stamp, and any packet wearing a fake stamp has it swapped for a plain one.

sections.title: Interior and Egress Node Behaviour
sections.content:
Interior nodes never undo a mark. They MUST NOT change not-PCN to anything else, NM to not-PCN, ThM to NM or not-PCN, or ETM to any other codepoint.

With two markings in use, a threshold-meter trigger makes the node change NM to ThM. An excess-traffic-meter trigger makes it change NM to ETM and also ThM to ETM. If both meters trigger, the excess-traffic rules MUST take precedence.

With only one marking in use, the unused meter SHOULD be disabled and MUST NOT mark. A node that sees the unexpected codepoint SHOULD raise a rate-limited management alarm. In excess-only mode a node changes a ThM packet to ETM when the meter fires. In threshold-only mode it MUST NOT change ETM to anything else. Appendix D explains the asymmetry: ETM is the more severe mark, and allowing an exception would need different data-plane code and be unsafe.

A PCN-egress-node SHOULD set the not-PCN codepoint (00) on all packets leaving the domain, unless it is certain that exposing other codepoints is safe under RFC 4774. If the domain uses only excess-traffic-marking, the egress MUST treat ThM as ETM. If only threshold-marking is used, it SHOULD treat ETM as ThM. Either case SHOULD raise a management alarm, since it signals a misconfiguration.
sections.plainLanguage: Once a packet has a warning stamp, nobody may wipe it off or make it milder. Only louder stamps can be added on the way.

sections.title: Compatibility with ECN and RFC 5696
sections.content:
The encoding follows BCP 124 (RFC 4774) by declaring that PCN-compatible DSCPs no longer carry default ECN semantics inside a PCN domain. A single IP header has no room for both end-to-end ECN and PCN marking, so end-to-end ECN has to be carried some other way, for example in the inner header of an IP-in-IP tunnel. Ingress nodes make sure the outermost ECN field is correct on entry, and egress nodes make sure packets leave with suitable ECN semantics, which stops ECN marks leaking in or out.

Because the encoding passed through the obsoleted RFC 5696 stage, misconfiguration may be more likely. The RFC suggests extra monitoring, for example an egress node watching for the onset of excess-traffic marking with no earlier threshold-marking, which may mean an interior node was set up to mark only ETM. The RFC says there is no known deployment of an RFC 5696 variant where the threshold meter set what is now the ETM codepoint.
sections.plainLanguage: The header bits are already used by another warning system. So the two systems are kept apart, with one inside a tunnel while the other works in the middle.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
PCN marks only mean something inside a PCN domain. The RFC assumes the domain is controlled by one operator, or by operators who trust each other. Inter-domain versions would have to be secure without that trust, but that is out of scope.

The main concern is spurious marks entering the domain, which can only happen if an ingress node is misconfigured. Depending on the edge behaviour, spurious marks lead to fewer flows being admitted or too many being terminated. The RFC expects good management to spot this quickly, since utilisation of the domain would fall rapidly.
sections.plainLanguage: The warning stamps are only trusted inside the club. If the front door guard makes a mistake, the club may turn away guests it did not need to.
